claims.text: Equiatomic FeNiCrMn is initially a single-phase FCC solid solution.
The initial FeNiCrMn structure has significant lattice distortion.
The initial structure contains no pre-existing vacancy clusters or HCP phases.
The yield strength of equiatomic FeNiCrMn is insensitive to strain rate from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
Yield strength decreases monotonically with increasing temperature.
At high strain rates, insufficient time for dislocation annihilation produces a high dislocation density.
Yield is controlled by thermally activated Shockley-partial nucleation at lattice-distortion sites.
Local potential-energy fluctuations caused by lattice distortion act as dislocation-nucleation sites.
Dislocation nucleation occurs at lattice-distortion sites rather than vacancy clusters.
The <11-1> orientation has a higher critical resolved shear stress and yield stress than the <110> orientation.
Slip-plane and slip-direction geometry in the <11-1> orientation maximizes the critical resolved shear stress for partial nucleation relative to <110>.
The geometric factor for partial dissociation is less favorable in <110>, resulting in lower yield stress.
At fixed temperature and strain rate, the <11-1> yield stress will exceed the <110> yield stress by more than 15%.
Strain-rate sensitivity will remain low for both tested orientations.
The HCP-like regions are intrinsic stacking faults bounded by Shockley partials rather than a transformed HCP phase.
CNA can distinguish atomic structures, and DXA can track dislocation motion in atomistic simulations.
Stacking-fault energy and local atomic coordination can distinguish an intrinsic stacking fault from an HCP phase.
Long-range order or distinct lattice parameters would indicate a true crystallographic transformation rather than a stacking fault.
Thermally activated nucleation dominates in single-phase FCC FeNiCrMn under the specified high strain rates.
Below 10^7 s^-1, dislocation-annihilation mechanisms may dominate.
